status_summary: DHS revoked Harvard's SEVP certification on 2025-05-22 and Proclamation 10948 (signed 2025-06-04, 90 FR 24493) suspended for six months entry of new Harvard F, M and J students, but a federal court blocked the revocation on 2025-06-20 and the proclamation on 2025-06-23, and DHS later stipulated it would not enforce the revocation. In late May 2025 the Secretary of State said the department would work with DHS to revoke visas of Chinese students with party ties or in critical fields and would add scrutiny to future applications from China and Hong Kong. DHS published a final rule on 2026-07-17 (91 FR 44976), effective 2026-09-15 subject to congressional review, replacing duration of status for F and J holders with fixed admission periods of up to four years; the parts read show no nationality-based limit for students. Entry limits for nationals of listed countries under Proclamations 10949 and 10998 are covered in c06-05.

timeline.event: DHS revoked Harvard's SEVP certification; Harvard sued the next day.

The Secretary of State said the department would work with DHS to revoke visas of Chinese students with Chinese Communist Party ties or in critical fields, and would revise criteria to add scrutiny to future applications from China and Hong Kong.

Proclamation 10948 (90 FR 24493, published 2025-06-10) suspended for six months entry of F, M and J nonimmigrants seeking to study at or join exchange programs at Harvard, and in section 3 directed State, Justice and Homeland Security to consider limiting Harvard's SEVP and SEVIS participation (pp. 24495-24496).

A federal district court issued a longer-term injunction against the Harvard proclamation; the SEVP revocation had been blocked on 2025-06-20, and DHS stipulated on 2025-08-06 that it would not enforce it.
DHS proposed replacing duration of status for F, J and I nonimmigrants with fixed admission periods.

DHS published the final fixed-period-of-admission rule (91 FR 44976) for F, J and I nonimmigrants, effective 2026-09-15 unless DHS publishes a notice changing the date after congressional review, and classified as a major rule; F and J admission is set to program length up to four years.

ICE proposes a rule (91 FR 64566) requiring SEVP-certified schools to pay a fee of $70,000 for a student's initial F-1 Optional Practical Training period and $30,000 for later periods before recommending it, citing fraud, protection of US workers and program integrity, and noting that reporting of foreign gifts to schools could help detect funding tied to foreign governments; the fee applies regardless of nationality. Comments are due 2026-11-09.

title: Put national security first in SEVP and cut student visas for adversary-country nationals
uncertainties: The Harvard litigation timeline comes from a science-policy organization's page last updated 2026-03-15, which lists the proclamation as expired and does not mention appeals. The NPR article does not state the announcement date; 2025-05-28 is taken from its URL. The final rule was read in large part: it caps F and J admission at program length up to four years and mentions an exception for some I nonimmigrants from the PRC, and no country-based limit for students was seen; whether it took effect on 2026-09-15 after congressional review was not confirmed. No source on the actual change in visa issuance to Chinese students was found. A DHS proposed rule of 2026-10-08 on Optional Practical Training fees is listed as context: it applies to all F-1 students regardless of nationality, rests mainly on fraud and worker-protection grounds with a secondary foreign-funding rationale, and does not change school certification, so it does not count toward the nationality-based visa cuts. The tail of that rule's text (regulatory flexibility and paperwork analyses) was not read. Proclamation 10948 and the final rule were confirmed through the Federal Register API and web text on 2026-10-18; the final rule web text was cut off after about 100,000 of 124,000 characters, so the regulatory text was not read in full and a nationality provision for students there cannot be excluded. The proclamation sets its own review of extension (section 2(e), 90 days) and, in section 3, only directs consideration of limiting SEVP participation; it does not itself end SEVP deference. State Department pages could not be opened, so the visa-scrutiny announcement rests on the news report.
